title: Architecture board — Conflux real-time sync service

masthead.headline: Pin the architecture on a real diagram, not a doc.
masthead.lede: This board holds one layered picture of the Conflux real-time editing backend — how the service is decomposed, how an edit flows through it, and which patterns are load-bearing. Author pins mark the decisions worth defending, and every claim carries where it came from — observed, inferred, or still open.

sections.label: Architecture
sections.title: The service in its own blueprint.

blocks.text: Each band below is one hop on the edit path, top to bottom. The tag inside a node says which tier it belongs to — the client, the stateless edge, a domain service, or persistence — so the four-tier decomposition survives even though the bands are ordered by hop.

blocks.title: One edit, from keystroke to durable op

nodes.label: Editor clients
nodes.note: browser editors, each holding an optimistic local CRDT replica so typing stays responsive before the server acknowledges
nodes.detail: A replica applies the keystroke locally, renders it, and only then sends the op. Every client is therefore briefly ahead of the server, and the merge engine is what makes those divergent replicas agree again rather than the client waiting to find out.

nodes.label: Realtime Gateway
nodes.note: stateless WebSocket edge; holds no document state, so any node serves any session behind a plain load balancer

nodes.label: Session Coordinator
nodes.note: routes each op to the right document actor and owns membership; the one place per-document ordering is decided
nodes.detail: One actor per open document, addressed by document id. Ordering is decided here and nowhere else, which is what lets the merge engine stay stateless about who sent what.

nodes.label: Presence Service
nodes.note: cursors and selections only, computed live and never written to the op log, so a lost presence update is harmless
nodes.detail: Holds an in-memory map of session to cursor, rebuilt from scratch whenever a gateway node restarts. Nothing here is worth persisting: a cursor that is one keystroke stale corrects itself on the next move.

nodes.label: CRDT Merge Engine
nodes.note: Yjs-style convergence with no central merge lock; concurrent edits merge deterministically and a slow client never blocks others

nodes.label: Op Log
nodes.note: append-only event store; every document state is reconstructable by replaying it, and this is the single authoritative record

nodes.label: Presence Bus
nodes.note: Redis pub/sub fan-out for presence with no durability guarantee; a dropped message just re-syncs on the next cursor move

nodes.label: Snapshot Store
nodes.note: a compacted, rebuildable cache of document state, always reconstructable from the op log and never authoritative on its own
nodes.detail: Written after every 500 ops so a cold open replays a bounded tail rather than the whole history. Deleting it costs a slow first load and nothing else.

sections.label: Provenance
sections.title: Every architecture claim carries its evidence status.

blocks.title: Reading the blueprint honestly
blocks.text: That clients already speak WebSocket to today's edge is measured from current traffic. The event-sourced op log is an architecture intent we chose for this service. Whether presence fan-out survives peak concurrency is still unresolved.

rows.text: Clients already hold a WebSocket to the current edge
Sampled from live gateway connection logs
Merge time, not transport, dominates perceived sync lag
A typical document holds a few thousand live ops in memory
The append-only op log is the single source of truth
A CRDT merge engine is used instead of OT

sections.label: Trade-offs
sections.title: What this architecture buys, and where it breaks.

rows.text: Scales horizontally; any node can serve any session with no sticky routing.
Every document state stays reconstructable and auditable by replay.
Removes the central merge lock, so a slow client never blocks everyone else's edits.
Grows per edit, so memory and payload cost more than compact OT deltas.
Adds a background job and a window where a snapshot lags the authoritative log.
A single document's in-memory CRDT state can outgrow one instance's memory budget.
One Redis channel saturates at very high concurrent-editor counts.

blocks.title: The numbers on this board are invented
blocks.text: The latency-budget proportions, the few-thousand live-ops figure, and any throughput or concurrency number implied by the diagram are illustrative shapes. Treat them as placeholders, not measured Conflux numbers, when building the service.

reply.heading: Send your decisions back to the coder.
reply.template:
# Feedback for the LLM coder

## Goal
Implement the Conflux real-time sync backend to the decomposition and data-flow decisions pinned on this board, before adding anything not shown here.

## Architecture at a glance
Four tiers, drawn one hop per band:
- Client — browser editors, each holding an optimistic local CRDT replica.
- Edge — a stateless Realtime Gateway over WebSocket; any node can serve any session.
- Domain — Session Coordinator (routes ops to a document actor, owns membership), CRDT Merge Engine (Yjs-style convergence, no central merge lock), Presence Service (ephemeral cursors and selections).
- Persistence — Op Log (append-only event store, single source of truth), Snapshot Store (derived, rebuildable cache), Presence Bus (Redis pub/sub, no durability).

## Edit data-flow
An edit is received at the gateway, routed by document id, merged by the CRDT engine, and appended to the op log. The gateway acks the client without waiting for the merge, and presence fans out without ever reaching the log. Perceived sync lag is dominated by merge time, not transport.

## Decisions to build to
- Gateway is stateless — hold no document state at the edge; scale horizontally behind a plain load balancer. (decided)
- CRDT merge over OT — accept extra per-edit metadata in exchange for a lock-free, convergent server. (approved)
- Op log is the source of truth — reconstruct any state by replaying the append-only log; treat snapshots as a derived cache only. (decided)

## Open questions — do not silently resolve
- Presence fan-out over a single Redis channel is unproven at peak concurrency; keep it behind a load test.
- The per-document in-memory CRDT budget is assumed, not measured; flag if a hot document could exceed one instance's memory.
